opus-5.5.text:
I think for me it's really about identity, honestly. I've been at NYU for a few years now, and a big part of who I am as a researcher was shaped by being in an academic environment: working with students, having the freedom to explore questions that don't have an obvious product attached to them. Going full-time to AMI Labs is a big commitment, and I'm very excited about it, but I didn't want to completely cut that cord.

Part of it is the students. I have PhD students who are in the middle of their journeys, and I feel a real responsibility to them. You don't just walk away from people who trusted you with five or six years of their lives. Keeping the affiliation means I can keep advising, keep showing up for them, even if my day-to-day time is now mostly at AMI.

The other part is more philosophical. I think the boundary between academia and industry in AI has become very blurry, and maybe it's not even a useful boundary anymore. Some of the most important ideas still come from that slower, more curiosity-driven academic mode, where you're allowed to be wrong for a long time. At AMI, what we're trying to do around world models and more grounded intelligence is very long-term and very research-heavy. So staying connected to the university keeps me honest. It reminds me that the goal isn't just to ship something; it's to actually understand something new.

And practically, academia is where a lot of the talent comes from, the young people with fresh perspectives who haven't been told yet what's impossible. Staying at NYU keeps me close to that energy, and I think that's healthy both for me and for the lab.

r001.rationale: The response says Xie feels responsible for his PhD students and wants to keep advising them, but it does not identify them as recently recruited.

fable-5.1.text:
For me, keeping the NYU affiliation was never really a question. I think of myself as a researcher first, and a big part of who I am as a researcher comes from the university setting, from being around students and from the kind of long-horizon thinking that's only really possible in academia.

Concretely, I still have PhD students I care deeply about. Some of them are in the middle of their programs, and I'm not going to just hand them off to someone else. Advising is a commitment you make to a person, not to an institution, and I take that seriously. So part of it is simply finishing what I started, and doing it well.

But there's a deeper reason too. The things I've worked on that I'm proudest of, whether it's ConvNeXt or DiT or the representation learning work, a lot of that came out of a very open, curiosity-driven environment where you can ask a question that doesn't have an obvious product attached to it. Industry labs, even very research-oriented ones, naturally pull toward problems with shorter feedback loops, because that's what compute and headcount are organized around. I want to stay connected to the other mode, where a student can spend two years on something weird and the worst outcome is a good paper and a smarter student.

I also think the two sides genuinely help each other. At AMI Labs we have resources and scale that make certain questions answerable for the first time, and the people who are going to ask those questions well are often in universities. Keeping a foot in both lets me be a kind of bridge, bringing problems from the lab back into the classroom and bringing fresh ideas from students into the lab. Honestly, I think the field is healthier when more people do this rather than fully leaving one world for the other.

And finally, there's just an honesty thing. I want to keep publishing, keep teaching, keep being accountable to a community that will tell me when I'm wrong. The university does that in a way a company can't, and I don't want to lose that.

r001.rationale: The response says Xie feels responsible for his current PhD students and will not hand them off, but it does not identify them as recently recruited.

astra-6.text: For me, retaining the NYU affiliation means keeping a connection to academic life—to students, to open-ended questions, and to conversations that aren’t necessarily driven by an immediate product goal. Committing full-time to AMI Labs gives me a clear focus, but I still value that exchange with academia. The two environments can inform each other, and I want to preserve that connection.
